lead: An automatic gearbox still has gears; electronics decide when to change and how hard to press the clutches. The transmission control unit (TCU) looks up the best gear in a shift map from throttle opening and vehicle speed, uses engine and shaft speeds to time the shift, and then commands solenoid valves that set hydraulic pressure. That pressure fills a clutch pack, so the new gear engages in a fraction of a second without a jolt. The same loop runs automated manuals, dual-clutch boxes, belt CVTs and conventional automatics. This chapter shows the loop, the hydraulics, and the four layouts.
prereq: You need: throttle, engine torque and power from electronic engine control, and speed and position sensors from automotive sensors and actuators.

sections.h3: The shift map and the shift schedule

blocks.text: The TCU needs two numbers before it can choose a gear: throttle opening α (percent, 0 means closed, 100 means wide open) and vehicle speed v (km/h, from the output shaft sensor or the wheel speed sensors).

Plot α on the vertical axis and v on the horizontal axis. Draw one curve for each shift. The region to the right of the 2→3 curve means the car is fast enough for third. The region to the left means drop back to second. The two boundaries are deliberately separated, so the box does not jump 2–3–2–3 at one steady speed. That separation is hysteresis, the same trick a thermostat uses.

Light throttle keeps the curves at low speed, so the car upshifts early and the engine stays slow and economical. Heavy throttle pushes the curves to high speed, so the engine is held near its power peak. Pressing the accelerator past a set fraction forces a downshift called kickdown. The family of curves for every gear is the shift schedule; the table stored inside the TCU is the shift map.
Every decision rests on one relation:

n<sub>engine</sub> is engine speed in rpm; n<sub>wheel</sub> is wheel speed in rpm; i<sub>gear</sub> is the selected gear ratio; i<sub>final</sub> is the final drive ratio. Both ratios are dimensionless.
An overdrive gear has i<sub>gear</sub> below 1, so it lowers engine speed. A low gear has i<sub>gear</sub> above 1 and multiplies torque.
A shift is hydraulic work. The TCU cannot push a clutch; it can only change a current.

items: Pressure stage. A regulator holds line pressure, the supply for the whole hydraulic circuit. A variable-force solenoid trims it. Line pressure must rise with engine torque, because a clutch carrying more torque needs more clamping force or it slips.
Fill stage. A shift solenoid opens and oil fills the piston of the on-coming clutch until the plates touch. This travel is the clutch fill; its time depends on oil temperature, oil age and clearance.

Torque stage. The off-going clutch releases while the on-coming clutch takes the load. If the off-going clutch lets go before the on-coming clutch can carry the torque, the engine flares (revs up with no load); if both clutches hold together for too long, they fight each other (tie-up) and the car jerks.

Torque reduction. The TCU asks the engine controller for a short torque cut, retarded spark or a small throttle trim, just as the ratio changes. The shift finishes faster and the passengers feel less of a step.

Learning. Speed sensors on the input and output shafts measure the real shift time. If the engine flared, the on-coming clutch was late, so the TCU lengthens its fill pulse or raises its pressure on the next shift; if the shift was harsh from tie-up, it shortens the fill or lowers the pressure. That is adaptive learning, and it repeats for the life of the box.

blocks.text: The same loop drives four different mechanisms.

items: AMT (automated manual). A normal manual gearbox with a robot that works the clutch and the gear lever. Cheap and efficient, but torque is interrupted, so the car nods.
DCT (dual-clutch transmission). Two clutches, one for odd gears and one for even. The next gear is already engaged, so the shift is a clutch-to-clutch handover with no torque break.
CVT (continuously variable transmission). A steel belt runs between two pulleys whose widths are set by hydraulic pressure. There are no steps; the TCU chooses the engine speed it wants.
Conventional automatic. Planetary gearsets with clutch packs, usually behind a torque converter.

blocks.text: The torque converter is an engine-driven impeller throwing oil at a turbine on the gearbox input, so the car can creep at idle with no mechanical link. It multiplies torque while the speed difference is large. At cruising speed a lock-up clutch closes inside the converter, tying input to engine and removing the slip loss. Many TCUs run the lock-up clutch with a small controlled slip (partial lock-up), which damps engine torsional vibration at low engine speed; the shift clutches do the ratio work.

figure.caption: The worked example on the shift map. At 60 km/h and 30 % throttle the car sits right of the downshift line, in top gear; pressing to 90 % moves it left of that line, so the TCU kicks down to direct gear and the engine speed rises from 1300 to 1857 rpm.

spec.aria: Shift map of throttle against speed with an upshift line and a dashed downshift line; point A at 60 km/h and 30 per cent, point B at 90 per cent; beside it the speed chain from wheel 530.5 rpm through final drive 3.50 to engine 1300 or 1857 rpm.

examples.question: A car runs at 60 km/h in top gear with 30 % throttle. Wheel radius r = 0.30 m, final drive ratio 3.50, top gear ratio 0.70. The driver presses the pedal to 90 % and the TCU kicks down to the direct gear (ratio 1.00). Find (a) the wheel speed in rpm, (b) the engine speed in top gear, (c) the engine speed after the kickdown, and (d) the rise in engine speed.
steps: Convert speed to SI: v = 60 ÷ 3.6 = 16.67 m/s.
Engine speed in top gear = 530.5 × 3.50 × 0.70 = 530.5 × 2.45 = 1299.8 rpm, about 1300 rpm.
Engine speed in the direct gear = 530.5 × 3.50 × 1.00 = 1856.8 rpm, about 1857 rpm.

Why the shift happens: on the shift map of Figure 5.1.1 the point (60 km/h, 30 %) lies right of the top-to-direct downshift line, but (60 km/h, 90 %) lies left of it, so the TCU selects the lower gear and the engine moves towards its power range.
examples.answer: Wheel speed 530.5 rpm; engine speed 1300 rpm in top gear and 1857 rpm after the kickdown to direct gear, a rise of 557 rpm at the same road speed.
examples.check:
import math
v = 60 / 3.6
r = 0.30
i_final = 3.50
i_top = 0.70
i_direct = 1.00
circ = 2 * math.pi * r
n_wheel = v / circ * 60
n_top = n_wheel * i_final * i_top
n_direct = n_wheel * i_final * i_direct
print(round(n_wheel, 1))
print(round(n_top))
print(round(n_direct))
print(round(n_direct - n_top))

traps: Leaving out the final drive when converting wheel speed to engine speed. Engine rpm needs both ratios: gear ratio and final drive.
Assuming a shift happens at a fixed vehicle speed. The map also reads throttle, so a light throttle upshifts early and a heavy one holds the gear.
Getting the ratio direction wrong. i<sub>gear</sub> above 1 reduces speed and multiplies torque; an overdrive below 1 does the opposite.
Confusing the lock-up clutch inside the torque converter with the shift clutches. Lock-up only removes converter slip; the shift clutches change the ratio.
Mixing rpm and rad/s, or forgetting the ×60 and ÷60 in the wheel-speed conversion.

quiz.q: Name the two inputs to the shift map.
quiz.a: Throttle opening α (percent) and vehicle speed v (km/h). Engine and shaft speeds are used to time and check the shift, not to choose the gear.

quiz.q: List the four transmission layouts controlled by a TCU.
quiz.a: AMT, DCT, CVT and the conventional automatic with a torque converter.

quiz.q: Why does the shift map use separate upshift and downshift curves?
quiz.a: The gap gives hysteresis. Without it the box would hunt between two gears whenever the speed sat on a single boundary.

quiz.q: Explain the fill stage and why the TCU has to learn it.
quiz.a: The fill stage is the oil volume needed to move the clutch piston until the plates touch. It depends on temperature, oil age and clearance, so it changes over life. The TCU times the shift with the speed sensors and adjusts the fill pulse, so the torque stage always starts at the right instant.

quiz.q: A car runs at 50 km/h, wheel radius 0.32 m, final drive 4.10, second gear 1.50. Find the engine speed.
After every upshift the engine speed flares and then drops. Which stage is failing, and what should the TCU change?
quiz.a: The fill stage is too short or line pressure too low, so the on-coming clutch is not ready when the off-going clutch releases, and the engine revs with no load. The TCU should lengthen the fill pulse or raise pressure, then verify with the measured shift time.

quiz.q: Why must line pressure rise as engine torque rises?
quiz.a: Clutch torque capacity grows with clamping force, and clamping force comes from hydraulic pressure. If engine torque exceeds capacity, the clutch slips, burns and the shift time drifts.

quiz.q: A CVT car accelerating at full throttle holds a nearly constant engine speed. Explain.
quiz.a: The TCU moves the pulley ratio continuously instead of stepping gears, so it can hold the engine at the speed of best torque or best fuel consumption while vehicle speed rises.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production TCUs now often sit in one powertrain controller shared with engine management, and the shift map is calibrated on a dynamometer over thousands of operating points. Hybrid and dual-clutch boxes add a torque-fill step: an electric motor or the pre-selected clutch covers the torque hole instead of the engine cutting torque. Research moves toward model-based pressure control and predictive shifting that reads the road ahead from navigation data. Useful search terms: shift quality calibration, adaptive clutch fill, torque-based shift control, DCT pre-selection.
